statement: The positive and negative predictive value of a diagnostic test (the probability that a positive/negative result is correct for a given patient) depends not only on the test's sensitivity and specificity but critically on the pre-test probability (disease prevalence) in the population tested; the same test yields a very different PPV in a high-prevalence versus a low-prevalence population.
effect_size: Worked example: a 99%-sensitive/99%-specific test applied to a disease with 0.1% prevalence yields PPV ~9% (about 10 false positives per true positive); the identical test at 10% prevalence yields PPV >90%.
population: Bayesian test-performance theory (probability identity, universally applicable)

provenance.primary: Lijmer JG, Bossuyt PMM — 'A readers' guide to the interpretation of diagnostic test properties: clinical example of sepsis', Intensive Care Med 2003
provenance.surfaced_via: PubMed esearch (pretest probability bayes diagnostic test) PMID 12734652

confidence_notes: This is a mathematical identity (Bayes' theorem), not an empirical finding — it is true by construction. Tier 'meta' used to denote highest certainty; direction 'supports' the proposition that pre-test probability governs result meaning. The single most load-bearing fact in test interpretation.

statement: A laboratory reference range is conventionally the central 95% of values in a presumed-healthy reference population, so by construction ~1 in 20 (5%) of healthy people fall 'out of range' on any single analyte; running a multi-analyte panel makes at least one false flag the expected outcome (e.g. ~64% probability of one or more flags on 20 independent analytes).

provenance.primary: Galen RS, Gambino SR — 'Beyond Normality: The Predictive Value and Efficiency of Medical Diagnoses', Wiley 1975; CLSI EP28-A3c reference-interval guidance
provenance.surfaced_via: Domain knowledge (lab-medicine standard); cross-ref WHAT-TO-TRACK-SYNTHESIS reference-range honesty

confidence_notes: Statistical identity given the 95% convention and independence assumption (real analytes are correlated, so true joint false-positive rate is somewhat lower than the independence estimate, but still high). Statistical-normal is not optimal and not healthy — three distinct concepts routinely conflated.

statement: Sensitivity and specificity are (approximately) intrinsic properties of a test that do not depend on disease prevalence, whereas predictive values do; high sensitivity makes a NEGATIVE result informative (SnNout) and high specificity makes a POSITIVE result informative (SpPin), and the positivity threshold trades one against the other.
effect_size: Likelihood ratios summarize the pair: LR+ = sens/(1-spec), LR- = (1-sens)/spec; LR+ >10 or LR- <0.1 = large, often conclusive shifts; LR near 1 = uninformative regardless of how abnormal the value looks.

provenance.primary: Sackett DL, Haynes RB, Guyatt GH, Tugwell P — 'Clinical Epidemiology: A Basic Science for Clinical Medicine'; Deeks JJ, Altman DG — 'Diagnostic tests 4: likelihood ratios', BMJ 2004
provenance.surfaced_via: Domain knowledge; PubMed LR literature (Sackett tradition)

confidence_notes: Sensitivity/specificity are only APPROXIMATELY prevalence-independent — they can shift with disease spectrum (spectrum bias) and verification bias. The SnNout/SpPin mnemonics are heuristics, strongest at extreme values.

statement: Screening low-pre-test-probability (healthy/asymptomatic) populations with broad or non-targeted testing generates predominantly false positives, because there are far more well people available to misflag than sick people to detect; this drives cascades (incidentaloma workups, benign biopsies, overtreatment) with documented physical, financial, and psychological harm and no demonstrated outcome benefit for untargeted broad screening of healthy adults.
effect_size: Direct consequence of low PPV at low prevalence (see predictive-value claim); harm is the cascade, not the single test.

provenance.primary: Welch HG — 'Less Medicine, More Health' / 'Overdiagnosed: Making People Sick in the Pursuit of Health' (2011)

confidence_notes: The mechanism (false-positive flood) is a mathematical certainty; the OUTCOME claim (net harm from untargeted broad screening) rests on observational/overdiagnosis evidence plus absence of benefit trials, which is strong but not RCT-per-panel. Targeted screening with proven benefit (e.g. colonoscopy, where pre-test reasoning and outcome trials exist) is explicitly excluded from this debunk.

statement: Population PSA screening produces at best a small reduction in prostate-cancer-specific mortality (ERSPC ~20% relative reduction, with large number-needed-to-screen/treat; other trials show little to none) at the cost of substantial overdiagnosis — detection and treatment of indolent cancers that would never have harmed the patient — making PSA the canonical example of the threshold/pre-test-probability problem rather than a clearly beneficial screen.
effect_size: ERSPC: ~20% relative reduction in prostate-cancer mortality; systematic review/meta-analysis: small, uncertain mortality benefit with significant overdiagnosis and treatment-related harms (incontinence, impotence).
population: ERSPC RCT (~162,000 men) + Ilic BMJ 2018 systematic review/meta-analysis of PSA screening RCTs

provenance.primary: Schröder FH et al. — 'Screening and Prostate-Cancer Mortality in a Randomized European Study', NEJM 2009 (PMID 19297566); Ilic D et al. — 'Prostate cancer screening with PSA: a systematic review and meta-analysis', BMJ 2018 (PMID 30185521)

confidence_notes: Direction 'mixed' is correct: there IS a real mortality signal in the best trial, AND real overdiagnosis harm — both true, which is the point. PSA is prostate-specific, not cancer-specific (raised by BPH, prostatitis, cycling), so its specificity for cancer is poor. Cross-ref oncology-claims (section 25). Modern practice uses shared decision-making, not blanket screening.

statement: Most serum tumor markers (CA-125, CEA, CA 19-9, CA 15-3, etc.) are appropriate for monitoring a KNOWN cancer (treatment response, recurrence) but are poor general-population SCREENING tests, because their modest sensitivity and low specificity applied to low-prevalence populations yield low positive predictive value and a high false-alarm/cascade burden.
effect_size: A good monitoring marker (high pre-test probability, trend in known patient) is usually a bad screening test (low pre-test probability, single value) — the same marker at opposite ends of the prevalence spectrum.
population: Tumor-marker clinical-utility literature; screening-trial evidence (e.g. CA-125/ovarian)

provenance.primary: NACB/EGTM laboratory-medicine practice guidelines on tumor markers; ovarian-cancer screening trials (UKCTOCS, PLCO) showing no mortality benefit from CA-125-based screening
provenance.surfaced_via: Domain knowledge; Bayesian derivation from prevalence

confidence_notes: AFP+ultrasound surveillance in high-risk cirrhosis and a few defined high-risk contexts are legitimate screening exceptions because they raise pre-test probability — the rule is about the general low-risk population.

statement: Histopathology (tissue biopsy examined by a pathologist) is the diagnostic gold standard for cancer and many diseases and the reference against which imaging, blood markers, and liquid biopsies are validated — but it is not infallible: sampling error means a negative biopsy does not zero risk (NPV < 100%), and inter-observer variability among pathologists is real and quantifiable, worst for tumor GRADING and borderline lesions.
effect_size: Gleason grading agreement is good for clear high/low-grade tumors but materially weaker in the intermediate range where treatment decisions hinge; diagnosis is more reproducible than grading.
population: Pathology reproducibility studies; ISUP grading-system revisions (2005, 2014) and subsequent updates

provenance.primary: 'Prostate Cancer Grading: An Update', Urol Clin North Am 2026 (PMID 41266001); ISUP consensus conferences on Gleason grading
provenance.surfaced_via: PubMed esearch (interobserver variability gleason grading) PMID 41266001

confidence_notes: 'Gold standard' is a relative term — it is the best available reference, not ground truth. The inter-observer-variability finding is why second opinions change management more often than patients expect. Cross-ref oncology-claims (section 25).

statement: Multi-cancer early detection (MCED) liquid-biopsy tests (e.g. cell-free DNA methylation assays) can detect cancer signals and localize them from a single blood draw, but in screening populations the majority of positive results are false or unactionable (PATHFINDER PPV ~38-43%), and no randomized trial has yet demonstrated that MCED screening reduces mortality — a mechanism-plausible, outcome-unproven technology that must not be presented as a validated screen.
effect_size: PATHFINDER prospective cohort: cancer-signal-detected PPV ~38-43%; signal-of-origin prediction accurate in most true positives; mortality benefit not yet established (randomized trials ongoing).
population: PATHFINDER prospective cohort (~6,600 adults >=50), Galleri MCED test

provenance.primary: Schrag D et al. — 'Blood-based tests for multicancer early detection (PATHFINDER): a prospective cohort study', Lancet 2023
provenance.surfaced_via: PubMed esearch (PATHFINDER multicancer early detection) PMID 37805216

confidence_notes: Established/legitimate liquid-biopsy use IS in KNOWN cancer (ctDNA genotyping, minimal residual disease, recurrence monitoring) — high pre-test probability. The unproven use is screening healthy people. Direction 'mixed': real detection capability, unproven outcome. Cross-ref section 07/25.

statement: Direct-to-consumer broad blood panels run on validated, CLIA-certified assays (the legitimate ones) still cause net harm when ordered without an indication in low-pre-test-probability people, because the reference-range false-positive math and low PPV produce statistically-inevitable false flags and downstream cascades; the harm is structural (absence of pre-test reasoning), distinct from the outright analytical fraud exemplified by Theranos.
effect_size: Same Bayesian/reference-range mechanism as broad-screening-low-prevalence-false-positive-flood; Theranos = separate failure mode (assays did not work, results fabricated).
population: DTC laboratory market; Theranos as documented analytical-validity failure (2015-2022)

provenance.primary: Carreyrou J — 'Bad Blood' (2018) for Theranos; reference-range/Bayesian derivation for the legitimate-lab over-testing trap
provenance.surfaced_via: Domain knowledge; cross-ref section 18 A.6 DTC-genetics Bayesian trap

confidence_notes: Two distinct claims bundled for clarity: (1) Theranos = analytical/clinical-validity fraud (well documented, criminal convictions); (2) legitimate DTC labs = sound assays but the over-testing-without-pre-test-reasoning trap (mechanistic derivation, strong but not RCT). The lesson from Theranos is that analytical+clinical validity is the un-skippable hard part of lab medicine.

statement: A single isolated out-of-range laboratory value in an asymptomatic person with low pre-test probability usually does not indicate disease, because biological variation, assay imprecision (analytical CV), pre-analytical error (fasting, time of day, hemolysis, biotin and other interferents), and the 1-in-20 reference-range statistics make regression-to-normal on a repeat draw the most likely explanation; the correct first response to one mild flag is often to repeat it, not to treat or image it.
effect_size: Many immunoassays (hormones) carry 10-20%+ CV; changes smaller than the reference-change value are noise. Between-method bias means absolute values are not comparable across labs/platforms.

provenance.primary: Tietz / Henry's Clinical Diagnosis and Management by Laboratory Methods (assay imprecision, interferences, biological variation)
provenance.surfaced_via: Domain knowledge; cross-ref section 13 endocrine assay variability, WHAT-TO-TRACK-SYNTHESIS

confidence_notes: Applies to asymptomatic mild flags at low pre-test probability — a grossly abnormal value, or any abnormality with concordant symptoms/high pre-test probability, is a different situation and should not be dismissed. Trend on one lab/one method, not across providers.
